sections.heading: Constitutional Text & Key Clauses
Litigation Roadmap & Procedural Forum
sections.body:
Competent Forum: High Court under Article 226 (judicial review of legislative and executive action, challenge to vires) and Supreme Court under Article 136 (Special Leave Petition) / Article 32 (if fundamental rights are violated).
Standard of Judicial Scrutiny: Ultra vires doctrine, legislative competence (Lists I, II, III of Seventh Schedule), non-arbitrariness under Article 14, and procedural vires.
Locus Standi: Aggrieved party whose legal, statutory, or constitutional rights are infringed, or public-spirited person in representative actions where public interest is directly affected.

sections.heading: Doctrinal Architecture & Judicial Precedents
sections.body:
Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973): The Constitution is the supreme law of the land; constitutional provisions must be harmoniously construed to preserve its basic structure and core institutional balance.
Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980): Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles form the bedrock of the Constitution; institutional boundaries and constitutional discipline cannot be breached.

examples.title: Illustration 1 — Direct Application (Constitutional Guarantee / Power Upheld)
examples.body: State action or statutory exercise strictly satisfies the conditions laid down under Article 145 (Rules of Court, etc). The authority acts within constitutional bounds, respects procedural fairness, and advances the constitutional objective of The Union. Outcome: Action is held valid and enforceable by the Court.

examples.title: Illustration 2 — Boundary Condition / Breach (State Action Fails)
examples.body: An executive order or legislation violates or bypasses the express procedural conditions, jurisdictional threshold, or fundamental guarantees of Article 145. The action is tainted by manifest arbitrariness, lacks legislative competence, or ignores mandatory safeguards. Outcome: The Court strikes down the measure or issues a writ of certiorari / mandamus.

hypotheticals.question: Examine the constitutional validity of the impugned directive in light of Article 145 and settled Supreme Court jurisprudence. What relief, if any, can be granted?
hypotheticals.analysis:
1. Scrutinize the constitutional source of power: Does Article 145 grant plenary power, or is it conditioned by express safeguards, legislative competence, or fundamental rights?
2. Apply the doctrine of ultra vires and manifest arbitrariness: If the directive creates arbitrary exceptions or bypasses statutory provisions, it violates Article 14 and the mandate of Article 145.
3. Examine procedural compliance: Substantive and procedural requirements under the Constitution cannot be waived on mere grounds of administrative convenience.
4. Balance public interest vs constitutional discipline: Constitutional limitations always prevail over executive fiat.

misconceptions.trap: Treating Article 145 as a standalone provision divorced from the rest of the Constitution.
misconceptions.correction: The Constitution is an organic whole. Article 145 must be interpreted harmoniously with Part III Fundamental Rights, the Preamble, and basic structure doctrine.

misconceptions.trap: Writing only the article heading without deconstructing constitutional ingredients, procedural anchors, and landmark ratios.
misconceptions.correction: A comprehensive legal analysis requires full IRAC structure: statutory anatomy, proving ingredients, procedural forum, leading case ratio, and practical application.

misconceptions.trap: Confusing the scope of Article 32 (only Part III FRs) with Article 226 (FRs and any other purpose).
misconceptions.correction: Verify whether Article 145 falls in Part III or another Part before advising the choice of writ forum. Article 32 cannot be moved for non-Part III rights unless connected to a Fundamental Right breach.

questionsAndAnswers.question: Case Brief & Legal Assessment: Scope and Application of Article 145 (Rules of Court, etc)
questionsAndAnswers.answer:
I. ISSUE & CONSTITUTIONAL CONTEXT
Whether the State action, statutory enactment, or individual claim conforms to the constitutional mandate, procedural prerequisites, and substantive protections enshrined in Article 145 (Rules of Court, etc) of the Constitution of India.

II. RULE & STATUTORY ANATOMY
Article 145 is situated in The Union (Articles 52–151), governing the “The Union” dimension of Indian constitutional law.
The essential constitutional ingredients are:
1. (1) Subject to the provisions of any law made by Parliament, the Supreme Court may from time to time, with the approval of the President, make rules for regulating generally the practice and procedure of the Court including—
2. (a) rules as to the persons practising before the Court;
3. (b) rules as to the procedure for hearing appeals and other matters pertaining to appeals including the time within which appeals to the Court are to be entered;
4. (c) rules as to the proceedings in the Court for the enforcement of any of the rights conferred by Part III; (cc) rules as to the proceedings in the Court under article 139A];
5. (d) rules as to the entertainment of appeals under sub-clause (c) of clause (1) of article 134;
6. (e) rules as to the conditions subject to which any judgment pronounced or order made by the Court may be reviewed and the procedure for such review including the time within which applications to the Court for such review are to be entered;

III. PROCEDURAL ANCHOR & REMEDIAL FORUM
1. Competent Forum: High Court under Article 226 (judicial review of legislative and executive action, challenge to vires) and Supreme Court under Article 136 (Special Leave Petition) / Article 32 (if fundamental rights are violated).
2. Standard of Review: Ultra vires doctrine, legislative competence (Lists I, II, III of Seventh Schedule), non-arbitrariness under Article 14, and procedural vires.
3. Standing: Aggrieved party whose legal, statutory, or constitutional rights are infringed, or public-spirited person in representative actions where public interest is directly affected.

IV. JUDICIAL INTERPRETATION & AUTHORITY
In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) (1973) 4 SCC 225, the Supreme Court established that The Constitution is the supreme law of the land; constitutional provisions must be harmoniously construed to preserve its basic structure and core institutional balance.
Furthermore, in Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980) (1980) 3 SCC 625, the Court reaffirmed that constitutional guarantees are justiciable and binding upon all state functionaries.

V. APPLICATION TO FACT PATTERNS
To apply Article 145:
1. Verify whether the impugned measure falls within the scope of the article's textual command.
2. Check whether any express exceptions, provisos, or constitutional limitations apply.
3. Subject the measure to tests of proportionality and non-arbitrariness under Article 14. If an ingredient is missing or breached, the measure is unconstitutional.

VI. CONCLUSION
Article 145 stands as a vital constitutional checkpoint. Any state action in breach thereof is void and amenable to writ jurisdiction under Articles 32 and 226. Current through the 106th Amendment (2023).

questionsAndAnswers.question: Comprehensive Constitutional Written Submissions: Doctrinal Scheme & Judicial Evolution of Article 145 (Rules of Court, etc)
questionsAndAnswers.answer:
I. INTRODUCTION & CONSTITUTIONAL PHILOSOPHY
Article 145 of the Constitution of India, titled “Rules of Court, etc”, represents a critical cornerstone of India’s constitutional democracy. Situated within The Union (Articles 52–151), the provision balances state power with individual liberties and institutional accountability. The Constituent Assembly intended this provision to be an active, living guarantee rather than an ornamental declaration.
II. STATUTORY & DOCTRINAL DECONSTRUCTION
A forensic analysis of Article 145 reveals the following distinct constitutional limbs:
(a) Limb 1: (1) Subject to the provisions of any law made by Parliament, the Supreme Court may from time to time, with the approval of the President, make rules for regulating generally the practice and procedure of the Court including—
(a) Limb 2: (a) rules as to the persons practising before the Court;
(a) Limb 3: (b) rules as to the procedure for hearing appeals and other matters pertaining to appeals including the time within which appeals to the Court are to be entered;
(a) Limb 4: (c) rules as to the proceedings in the Court for the enforcement of any of the rights conferred by Part III; (cc) rules as to the proceedings in the Court under article 139A];
(a) Limb 5: (d) rules as to the entertainment of appeals under sub-clause (c) of clause (1) of article 134;
(a) Limb 6: (e) rules as to the conditions subject to which any judgment pronounced or order made by the Court may be reviewed and the procedure for such review including the time within which applications to the Court for such review are to be entered;
The Article must be read in conjunction with the foundational architecture of the Constitution:
1. Separation of Powers & Checks and Balances: No branch of government possesses untrammelled discretion.
2. Rule of Law & Non-Arbitrariness: Every exercise of authority under Article 145 must satisfy the basic standard of fairness and reasonableness.
3. Transformative Constitutionalism: The provision must be interpreted progressively to advance justice, liberty, and equality as pledged in the Preamble.
III. JURISPRUDENTIAL EVOLUTION & LEADING CASE LAW
The Supreme Court of India has deconstructed Article 145 across several seminal judgments:
1. Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) (1973) 4 SCC 225:
   Ratio Decidendi: The Constitution is the supreme law of the land; constitutional provisions must be harmoniously construed to preserve its basic structure and core institutional balance.
2. Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980) (1980) 3 SCC 625:
   Ratio Decidendi: Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles form the bedrock of the Constitution; institutional boundaries and constitutional discipline cannot be breached.
IV. PROCEDURAL ROADMAP & LITIGATION CHECKLIST (SENIOR COUNSEL REFERENCE)
When approaching the Court under or in respect of Article 145:
1. Forum Selection: High Court under Article 226 (judicial review of legislative and executive action, challenge to vires) and Supreme Court under Article 136 (Special Leave Petition) / Article 32 (if fundamental rights are violated).
2. Pleading Essentials: The writ petition or plaint must specifically plead:
   (a) The exact constitutional authority or violation under Article 145;
   (b) The factual narrative establishing how each statutory ingredient is satisfied or infringed;
   (c) The absence of an effective alternative remedy, or justification under the Whirlpool Corporation exceptions (breach of fundamental rights, violation of natural justice, or complete lack of jurisdiction).
3. Evidentiary Standard: Discharge of burden under BSA ss. 104–106 and production of certified records.
V. IRAC PROBLEM ANALYSIS (PRACTICE HYPOTHETICAL)
Fact Matrix: The State issues a notification encroaching upon the domain of Article 145 without satisfying statutory preconditions.
Issue: Does the executive notification violate the constitutional guarantees and procedures of Article 145?
Rule: Under Article 145, state action is strictly conditioned by constitutional provisions and cannot be exercised arbitrarily.
Application: The impugned notification fails because it circumvents the procedural safeguards and lacks rational nexus to the constitutional objective. Applying the proportionality test, the State has failed to adopt the least intrusive means.
Conclusion: The notification is unconstitutional and void ab initio. The appropriate writ of certiorari or mandamus shall issue.
VI. CRITICAL APPRAISAL & CURRENT-LAW MILESTONE
Article 145 remains a vibrant instrument of governance, current through the 106th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2023. A robust democracy requires rigorous adherence to its letter and spirit to protect the citizen against executive overreach and legislative excesses.

enhancement.definition: ARTICLE 145 of the Constitution of India establishes the constitutional regime governing Rules of Court, etc. Situated in Part V: The Union (Chapter IV: The Union Judiciary (Articles 124–147)), it provides binding constitutional norms, institutional allocations of power, and mandatory substantive and procedural safeguards that constrain State action.

(a) rules as to the persons practising before the Court;

examples: Factual scenario (Constitutional Compliance): An authority acts strictly within the procedural and substantive bounds of ARTICLE 145, issuing a reasoned order after satisfying all conditions precedent. On judicial review, the High Court upholds the measure, confirming that the exercise of power conforms to Part V: The Union and constitutional safeguards.

Factual scenario (Ultra Vires Action): An authority bypasses the mandatory statutory prerequisites under ARTICLE 145, acting arbitrarily or in excess of constitutional competence. The Supreme Court intervenes, holding that constitutional limitations cannot be sacrificed for administrative expediency, and quashes the impugned action.
distinctions: ARTICLE 145 vs General Administrative Power: Powers exercised under ARTICLE 145 derive directly from the Constitution and enjoy supremacy over ordinary statutes and subordinate rules.

ARTICLE 145 vs Fundamental Rights in Part III: Any measure enacted or executed under ARTICLE 145 remains subordinate to the Fundamental Rights guaranteed under Articles 14, 19, and 21 unless expressly protected by a saving clause.
problemApplication: Issue: Whether an order passed in purported exercise of power under ARTICLE 145 without fulfilling statutory conditions precedent is constitutionally valid.
Rule: Exercise of constitutional authority under ARTICLE 145 requires strict adherence to mandatory procedural and substantive conditions precedent.
Application: The record reveals that the authority acted without recording requisite satisfaction and bypassed procedural safeguards mandated by Part V: The Union.
Counterargument: The State asserts broad executive discretion and administrative necessity.
Conclusion: The impugned order is ultra vires ARTICLE 145 and void for manifest arbitrariness under Article 14.
